title: Small firms and why they survive

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain what makes a firm small, why small firms survive beside large ones, what they contribute, and trace what a supermarket opening does to a town's small shops.

blocks.heading: What makes a firm small
blocks.text: A small firm employs few workers, produces a small output and usually serves a local market, with the owner often running it directly. Marula Foods in Oshakati is a working example: 6 workers press marula fruit into 9 000 bottles of juice a year and sell them to 15 shops within 60 km of the plant. Where the line sits between small and large differs between countries and industries - one uses the worker headcount, another yearly sales or the capital the firm uses - so smallness is a judgement against a measure, not one fixed headcount.

blocks.heading: Why small firms survive, and what they add
blocks.text: Small firms often survive beside large ones because they sell what large firms find hard to copy. Where a shopper values being known by name, the corner shop's owner remembers the account; where a narrow group of customers wants something particular, a small firm serves a niche too thin for a large firm to bother with. Flexibility counts too: a small firm changes its stock within days. What they add follows from that survival: jobs in places large firms do not reach, training for workers who may later start firms of their own, and spending kept circulating locally - though the wages and job security they offer tend to lag behind those of large firms.

blocks.heading: When a supermarket opens at the edge of town
blocks.text: In 2025 a large supermarket opened at the edge of Oshakati, near the streets where the town's small shops trade. The chain runs from its buying power: bulk purchases put its prices below the small shops', and the range under one roof is wider. Customers respond, so the small shops nearby are likely to lose revenue. Some change what they do - opening longer, delivering, stocking what the supermarket does not carry - and may hold enough trade to keep going; those that meet it head-on on price are the most exposed. In Vietnam, family-run food stalls keep trading beside convenience chains for the same reason: speed and familiarity are things a chain cannot easily supply.

blocks.heading: The challenges small firms face
blocks.text: Small firms also face challenges that large firms feel less. Finance comes first: a small firm has few assets to offer as security and a short trading record, so lenders see more risk and tend to lend less, at higher interest, or not at all, and growth is often limited to what the owner can save. Costs come second: buying in small quantities earns no bulk discount, and fixed costs such as rent are spread over a small output, so average costs tend to be higher than a large rival's. A small bakery in Rundu paying N$9 a kilogram for flour, against N$7 for a national chain buying by the truckload, starts each loaf at a disadvantage. Competition comes third: a supermarket or national chain can undercut on price and outspend on advertising. Finally, much rests on the owner: illness or one poor decision can stop the firm, and a fall in demand in its one town hits it harder than a firm selling across the country.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The demand that keeps a small firm's niche alive is examined in topic 2.3, and the spending households bring to these shops is the subject of topic 3.2.
